chunks: "Ripple matters in proportion to how much the load notices it, so it matters least when the load has a wide tolerance, rejects it, or averages it. Wide-tolerance loads first: a 3.
3 volts digital rail that allows plus or minus 10% has 330 millivolts of margin each way, so 17 millivolts peak-to-peak of ripple uses about 8.
5 millivolts of it, under 3%, and I could tolerate 50 or 100 millivolts.
Second, loads behind another stage: if the buck feeds an LDO with 30 decibels of PSRR at the switching frequency, 17 millivolts becomes 0.
5 millivolts, so the buck ripple only needs to keep the LDO from running out of headroom.

Third, loads that average: a heater has a thermal time constant of seconds, a motor winding is an inductor that filters the pulses, an LED driven by current only changes average brightness, and 500 kilohertz is invisible.
Fourth, loads that are only measuring DC.
So in those cases I'd take a bigger ripple ratio, 40 or 50% instead of 20 to 30, which allows a smaller inductor and fewer capacitors, lower cost and faster transients.
What I'd still check is peak current against saturation, the EMI, and that the larger ripple doesn't push the converter into DCM too early."
